tldr: We proposed TouchTherm, a framework that builds simulation-ready multimodal digital twins of real-world objects, simultaneously rendering high-fidelity tactile textures and time-varying thermal distributions.
hero_caption: Overall concept of TouchTherm. From real-world object observations, it constructs simulator-ready assets that integrate a coarse collision mesh, local micro-height fields for optical tactile sensors, and a dynamic thermal field capturing heat diffusion and cooling.
overview:
For robots to perform dexterous manipulation in the real world, experiencing diverse contacts in physical simulators is essential. However, conventional 3D models only capture visual color and coarse geometry (collision meshes). They completely miss the millimeter- and micrometer-scale fine details that tactile sensors pick up, as well as the temperature changes felt upon touching an object.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed TouchTherm, a pipeline that automatically constructs visuo-tactile-thermal digital twins from real-world scans. The key insight is decoupling computationally heavy micro-details from the collision mesh, storing them instead as tangent-space height fields queried only during indentation by optical tactile sensors (such as GelSight). In addition, by recording the cooling process after heating with infrared cameras and pairing it with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) based on the heat equation, they learn a surface thermal diffusion model capable of simulating surface temperatures in real time at any given moment.

Evaluations across 20 everyday objects demonstrated that synthesized tactile images closely match real sensor outputs. Classifiers trained purely on simulated tactile images recognized real-world tactile observations with high accuracy (Sim-to-Real). Furthermore, user studies with a thermal-feedback VR glove confirmed that humans can realistically perceive the coldness and warmth of virtual objects.
contributions: Established a simulator-ready multimodal digital twin pipeline integrating visual geometry, tactile micro-height fields, and dynamic thermal fields into a unified coordinate frame.

Proposed a contact-conditioned tactile rendering method that separates coarse collision meshes from high-frequency tactile textures, achieving high-fidelity optical tactile simulation without computational overload.

Constructed a real-time deployable dynamic thermal field model by identifying surface thermal diffusion and environmental heat dissipation parameters from multiview infrared videos using physics-informed neural networks.
Demonstrated downstream utility across 20 diverse objects, including Sim-to-Real tactile object recognition and thermal feedback delivery via a VR glove, alongside rigorous quantitative benchmarks.

sections.heading: Bringing Touch and Temperature to Robots: A New Step for Digital Twins
sections.summary: Current simulators focus primarily on vision and coarse collision geometry, lacking fine tactile details and dynamic temperature cues. This paper introduces TouchTherm, an asset creation pipeline integrating micro-surface structures and dynamic thermal fields for robotic simulation.
sections.details:
Simulation is an indispensable tool in robot learning, but the reality gap remains a major barrier when deploying models to the physical world. One primary reason is that in contact-rich manipulation tasks, virtual objects offer sensory feedback restricted almost entirely to visual cues and coarse forces.

Faithfully reproducing real-world interactions presents two main challenges:
- The trade-off between capturing micro-scale geometry and computational representation: Fine structures such as shallow grooves and embossed patterns fundamentally shape the signals of optical tactile sensors. However, incorporating them directly into high-polygon meshes causes vertex counts to explode, breaking collision detection and physics simulation.
- The absence of dynamic thermal fields: An object's temperature is non-uniform across materials and geometry, varying over time as it is touched or left to cool. Simply assigning a single static temperature label is insufficient for tactile material identification or immersive VR experiences.

TouchTherm resolves these challenges. It relies on a manageable coarse mesh for collision handling, queries local tangent-space height fields during tactile rendering, and overlays a physics-grounded dynamic thermal field. This approach successfully balances computational efficiency with rich expressive detail.

sections.heading: From Seeing to Feeling: Moving to Multimodal Assets
sections.summary: Existing 3D datasets and reconstruction methods like NeRF focus on visual geometry, leaving tactile and thermal information largely absent. TouchTherm bridges this gap by unifying coarse collision meshes, local micro-geometry, and dynamic thermal fields in a single object coordinate frame.
sections.details:
### The State of Multimodal Data Collection
Thanks to 3D scanners, multiview stereo (MVS), and recent neural rendering techniques like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, reconstructing visual geometry and surface appearance has reached a mature stage. In parallel, research exploring non-visual sensing with tactile sensors and thermal cameras has grown. However, most efforts collect only localized, isolated observations rather than reusable assets anchored to complete object geometry.

### Challenges in Datasets and Simulation Assets
Well-known datasets such as YCB and Google Scanned Objects are widely used in robotic grasping benchmarks, but they do not capture tactile-scale micro-structures or transient temperature dynamics. While newer efforts like ObjectFolder integrate acoustic and tactile observations, they still do not handle time-varying 3D thermal fields.

Furthermore, tactile simulators (such as TacSL and Taxim) face a dilemma: feeding them high-resolution meshes degrades simulation speed dramatically. TouchTherm reconciles efficiency and realism by organizing coarse collision geometry, registered micro-height fields, and dynamic thermal fields under a shared representation.

sections.heading: Weaving Geometry, Touch, and Heat: The TouchTherm Pipeline
sections.summary: Data collection combines structured-light scanning, photometric stereo for normal estimation, and multiview infrared video. For tactile sensing, Poisson reconstruction produces micro-height fields, while a PINN identifies surface diffusion parameters to enable real-time thermal simulation.
sections.details:
### Pipeline Overview and Hardware Setup (III-A, III-B)
The TouchTherm pipeline begins with geometric scanning, surface normal capture, and infrared recording. A handheld structured-light scanner (EinScan Pro 2X V2) acquires the coarse full-body mesh. Multiview surface normal maps are estimated from smartphone images taken under varying illumination using a pretrained model (SDM-UniPS). For thermal data, multiple synchronized infrared cameras capture the natural cooling process after heating the object with a heat gun.

### Tactile Micro-Geometry Reconstruction and Rendering (III-C)
The micro-geometry pipeline decouples collision geometry from tactile details:
- Normal Map Registration: Camera poses are solved via Perspective-n-Point (PnP) using 2D-to-3D feature correspondences between normal images and the 3D mesh.
- Tangent-Space Projection and Height Field Recovery: At a contact point $\mathbf{p}$, a local tangent frame is defined and a surface patch is sampled. Projecting the normal map yields local surface gradients, and solving Poisson's equation via a discrete cosine transform (DCT) recovers the micro-height field $h_{\mu}$.
- Contact-Conditioned Synthesis: In simulation (Isaac Sim / TacEx), the micro-height field is weighted by a contact mask $M$ and a physical calibration scale $\gamma$, then added to the low-frequency indentation $H_0$ from the coarse mesh. This produces sharp tactile imprints the moment an elastomeric sensor indents the surface, without increasing collision overhead.

### Dynamic Thermal Field Reconstruction via Physics Regularization (III-D)
The thermal model identifies two key physical parameters: the surface diffusion coefficient $\alpha$ and the ambient thermal relaxation coefficient $h$.
- Multiview Integration: Infrared temperature readings are corrected for viewing angle attenuation and temperature drift, then projected and averaged across surface point clouds.
- Graph Diffusion Operator: Using Gaussian weights over $k$-nearest neighbors, a graph Laplacian $\mathbf{L}$ is constructed to approximate surface heat diffusion across the mesh.
- Simultaneous Identification with PINNs: A multilayer perceptron (MLP) models the continuous temperature field, trained to jointly minimize data error and physics residuals of the heat diffusion equation. This physically regularizes unobserved areas while identifying the optimal $\alpha$ and $h$.
- Runtime Deployment: After parameter identification, the neural network is discarded. Inference switches to an explicit forward Euler matrix formulation, enabling extremely lightweight, real-time temperature propagation.

sections.heading: Extensive Validation: From Tactile Fidelity to Sim-to-Real and VR
sections.summary: Evaluations across 20 everyday objects show tactile rendering fidelity far exceeding baselines, while the dynamic thermal field achieves a surface temperature MAE of $0.592~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at 45 seconds. The assets also successfully enable Sim-to-Real tactile recognition and VR thermal feedback.
sections.details:
### Asset Construction and Tactile Appearance Evaluation (IV-A, IV-B)
Experiments covered 20 objects spanning planar, curved, and free-form geometries across varied materials, including a wooden box, a seal stamp, a coin, and a computer mouse. Asset construction took approximately half a day per object modality.
Simulation fidelity against real GelSight Mini tactile observations was evaluated using Gradient SSIM (G-SSIM) and High-Frequency Normalized Cross-Correlation (HF-NCC). While sensor-to-sensor variance on real hardware (Real–Real) yielded G-SSIM of $0.0954$ and HF-NCC of $0.1622$, TouchTherm (Real–Sim) reached $0.0712$ and $0.0775$.
Ablation studies demonstrated that the proposed method (Ours: 0.0701 / 0.0911) captured real-world micro-details significantly better than coarse geometry alone (0.0480 / 0.0116) or direct image-space height integration (0.0629 / 0.0081).

### Prediction Accuracy of Dynamic Thermal Fields (IV-C)
Evaluating predictions against held-out views showed a surface-temperature mean absolute error (MAE) of $0.465~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at 30 s and $0.592~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at 45 s, closely tracking the cooling trajectory. Ablations revealed that the relaxation parameter $h$ drives global temperature decay, whereas the surface diffusion coefficient $\alpha$ is critical for smoothing local temperature gradients.

### Downstream Task Validation (IV-D)
- Sim-to-Real Tactile Object Recognition: A ResNet-18 was trained exclusively on simulated GelSight images and tested on 400 real sensor images (20 per object). A model trained on coarse geometry achieved only $20.0\%$ Top-1 accuracy, while TouchTherm assets raised accuracy to $34.0\%$ (Top-3 accuracy: $63.0\%$, Macro-F1: $29.3\%$). This confirms that micro-scale surface cues provide valuable discriminative signals for real-world tactile recognition.
- VR Thermal Feedback: A system combining a Meta Quest 3 headset and temperature-controlled thermoelectric Peltier pads allowed 10 human participants to touch virtual objects. It received high ratings for visuo-thermal alignment (6.30/7.0) and sense of presence (6.10/7.0), demonstrating that spatiotemporally varying thermal feedback can be presented naturally.

sections.heading: Looking Ahead: Toward Full Physical Interaction
sections.summary: TouchTherm successfully combines coarse meshes, tactile height fields, and dynamic thermal fields into simulation-ready multimodal assets. Current micro-geometries are dedicated to optical tactile rendering, leaving contact mechanics and bidirectional heat transfer as key future directions.
sections.details:
TouchTherm provides a comprehensive framework to extract visual geometry, tactile micro-structures, and dynamic thermal fields from real objects, turning them directly into simulation-ready assets. Across 20 objects, it proved effective in producing realistic tactile rendering, accurate temperature forecasting, Sim-to-Real tactile recognition, and immersive VR thermal feedback.

The authors also outline several current limitations:
- Micro-scale height fields are used exclusively for optical tactile rendering, without directly affecting physical contact mechanics such as grasping dynamics or local friction changes.
- The thermal formulation models passive natural cooling; it does not yet simulate bidirectional heat exchange, such as localized heat transfer when warm robot fingers or human hands make contact.

Future work aims to connect micro-geometry with compliant contact and friction models, as well as to simulate full bidirectional heat transfer during physical contact.

takeaways: Decoupling low-frequency collision meshes from high-frequency tactile textures enables high-fidelity optical tactile rendering without compromising simulation speed.
Applying physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to multiview infrared video identifies surface heat diffusion parameters, allowing fast forward-Euler numerical integration during runtime.
Synthesizing high-detail tactile textures in simulation significantly improves Sim-to-Real tactile object recognition accuracy without requiring any real-world training images.
limitations: Micro-height fields are used solely for tactile image synthesis and do not influence physical mechanics such as friction or micro-slip.
The thermal model approximates natural cooling and cannot simulate bidirectional heat transfer when hands or robotic grippers absorb or supply heat upon contact.
Object scanning, multiview capture, and 2D-to-3D alignment still involve manual annotation steps, falling short of a fully automated large-scale pipeline.
